name: SFX Variation And Exaggeration
use_when: A transition, punch-in, shake, meme beat, physical action, or reveal needs extra impact.
The edit feels visually active but sonically flat.
A repeated motion needs a family of related SFX instead of one identical whoosh.
Text, icon, zoom, or transition movements need short-form whooshes, hits, or reverse hits.
An AE-animated Reel needs SFX after the animation render is aligned in Premiere.
A visually polished YouTube edit feels flat and needs a focused SFX spotting pass.
A human cutaway needs subtle physical texture such as footsteps, cloth, object, or surface sound.
An infographic sequence needs soft cues for title entrances, route traces, highlights, chart bars, or screenshot swaps.
A premium brand intro needs hits, pops, ticks, or drum accents locked to logo, text, flicker, underline, or camera events.
A text flicker, font-shift, number counter, outline reveal, highlight wipe, glow sweep, or staggered reveal needs a tiny tick, click, shimmer, or glitch cue that makes the change feel intentional.
An anime/action edit needs clip-specific whooshes, impacts, textures, or short identity voice lines to make motion and character moments land.
avoid_when: The subject tone is serious and SFX would cheapen it.
The effect competes with dialogue or testimony.
The visual action is already clear and the sound would become clutter.

timeline_pattern.variation_rule: Rotate similar SFX variations for repeated movements so the edit does not sound copied and pasted.
timeline_pattern.exaggeration_rule: Use oversized sounds for comedy or emphasis only when the tone supports it.
timeline_pattern.library_rule: Build reusable SFX folders by job: whoosh, hit, pop, riser, ambience, meme, texture, and transition.
timeline_pattern.foley_rule: For organic social moments, context-specific foley should be subtle enough to sell realism without calling attention to itself.
timeline_pattern.finishing_rule: Add SFX as a dedicated finishing pass after visual motion is locked enough to place cues frame-accurately.
timeline_pattern.anticipation_rule: Use a reversed hit before a question, reveal, or transition when the edit needs anticipation.
timeline_pattern.isolation_rule: Temporarily muting dialogue and music can help spot SFX opportunities, but the full mix must be restored and checked afterward.
timeline_pattern.infographic_rule: For documentary graphics, prioritize major reveal/highlight cues over constant whooshes on every layer.
timeline_pattern.intro_frame_lock_rule: For premium intros, remove any cue that does not land on a visible logo, text, flicker, underline, camera, cut, or transition event.
timeline_pattern.voice_line_rule: Use short identity voice lines only when they clarify character, emotion, or impact; do not place them on every clip by habit.
timeline_pattern.text_tick_rule: For flicker, font-shift, highlight, glow, or staggered reveal text, cut and retime the cue so it ends with the visual change instead of continuing under the next line.

motion.rule: SFX should land on the actual motion start, impact, or reveal frame, not randomly near it.

sound.rule: Layer SFX under speech conservatively and fade tails that distract from the next line.

keyframe_values.sync_tolerance: Aim to land hits within 1-2 frames of the visual impact for energetic edits.
keyframe_values.variation_count: Keep at least 3-5 variants for common whooshes or hits in a reusable library.
keyframe_values.whoosh_start_level: Start whooshes around -10 dB below dialogue, then adjust by ear and context.
keyframe_values.dialogue_priority: Lower, shorten, or remove SFX when they mask story-critical words.
keyframe_values.isolated_pass: After solo SFX spotting, lower cues in the restored full mix until they support motion without becoming annoying.
keyframe_values.foley_level: For subtle foley under dialogue, start 12-18 dB below speech and raise only until the movement feels believable.
keyframe_values.infographic_level: Start infographic ticks, whooshes, and shutter cues around -12 dB below narration, then lower if the section feels busy.
keyframe_values.premium_intro_sync: For precision intro hits, aim for 0-1 frame sync on the visible event and use a 4-12 frame duck or fade into body speech.
keyframe_values.text_flicker_tick: For very fast text flickers, align ticks to opacity or font-change frames and shorten/speed the cue so the tail clears with the flicker.
keyframe_values.staggered_glitch_reveal: For staggered text reveals, align the glitch cue to the first visible word change and trim it at the final word's reveal frame.
keyframe_values.amv_voice_line: Start identity voice lines at or just before the clip's opening beat when they are used as a character anchor.

captions.rule: Do not combine loud SFX with busy caption animation unless the moment is intentionally high-energy.

color.rule: No direct color rule; flashes or shakes paired with SFX must preserve action readability.

implementation.ffmpeg: Align SFX clips by frame in the EDL, apply afade at starts/ends, and use volume filters to keep dialogue clear.
implementation.remotion: Trigger SFX from the same frame constants that drive punch-ins, shakes, reveals, or caption pops.
implementation.blender: Use audio markers for camera shakes, object impacts, and reveal timing.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Use separate SFX tracks, rotate effect variants, and manually align hits to motion frames. For text flickers, font shifts, highlight wipes, glow sweeps, or staggered reveals, cut the tick/click/glitch cue and use blade/speed controls so it ends with the text animation. Import local cues through Sounds > Device when needed and review them with the full song restored.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Use SFX bins by job, markers for impact frames, clip gain, and short fades on every effect. For a focused pass, temporarily mute dialogue/music while spotting, then unmute and rebalance. For AE roundtrips, import the animation render first, then place whooshes, hits, typewriter cues, camera sounds, and reward sounds against visible motion.

common_mistakes: Using the same whoosh on every transition.
Using generic foley that does not match the visible surface or movement.
Adding an SFX cue to every small infographic layer until the documentary tone feels cheap.
Adding SFX because the effect exists rather than because the beat needs sound.
Letting meme sounds overpower the story or date the edit.
Leaving hard SFX edges without fades.
Letting whooshes sit at the same level as dialogue in a dense short-form edit.
Adding SFX before the animation timing is locked and then leaving cues out of sync.
Placing SFX while other tracks are muted and forgetting to re-check dialogue/music masking.
Adding intro SFX because they sound premium even though no visible event justifies them.
Leaving a ticking, shimmer, or glitch cue running after the text visual has ended.
Adding character voice lines or intense impacts to every clip until the edit loses contrast.
qc: Does every SFX cue have a named visual or story job?
Does any foley cue match a visible or strongly implied movement and stay below dialogue?
Do infographic cues map to major visible reveals and stay below narration?
Do repeated movements use variation instead of the exact same file every time?
Do SFX peaks stay below dialogue?
Do hits land within 1-2 frames of the intended impact when sync matters?
Are serious sections free from tone-breaking default whooshes?
Are whooshes low enough that speech stays dominant?
Does any reversed hit build into a real question, reveal, or transition?
Were SFX placed against the final visible animation render?
After any isolated SFX pass, was the full mix restored and checked?
In a premium intro, does every cue land on a visible event and preserve proof or body speech?
For flicker, font-shift, highlight, glow, or staggered text, does the cue end with the visual change and stay below speech?
In an anime/action edit, do voice lines and SFX clarify the clip rather than clutter every beat?
